variants.title: Work the framework in order
variants.context: The seven-step framework runs from the product contract, through ML framing, data and evidence, model strategy, evaluation and safety, the critical paths, and finally operations. Each step produces an artifact that constrains the next, which is what stops the answer from starting at a model choice.
variants.prompt: An interviewer opens with a vague prompt: build a generative assistant for our customers. Put the first five steps in order.

items.text: Frame the ML behavior: inputs, outputs, acceptable uncertainty, retrieval or generation needs, and success criteria.
Clarify the product contract: users, tasks, modalities, latency, risk, privacy, volume, and explicit non-goals.
Define evaluation and safety: deterministic checks, task metrics, calibrated judges, red teams, and human review.
Design data and evidence: sources, permissions, labeling, freshness, lineage, evaluation sets, and feedback capture.
Select the model strategy: compare prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, tool use, and model tiers against the constraints.

variants.hint: Each step hands the next one an artifact it cannot proceed without.
variants.explanation: The order exists to prevent premature model selection: requirements shape evaluation, and evaluation shapes data and model choices.

variants.title: Work the framework in order
variants.context: The seven-step framework runs from the product contract, through ML framing, data and evidence, model strategy, evaluation and safety, the critical paths, and finally operations. Each step produces an artifact that constrains the next, which is what stops the answer from starting at a model choice.
variants.prompt: The product brief already fixes the contract and the ML framing for an image generation product. Put the remaining five steps in order.

items.text: Select the model strategy: compare diffusion variants, prompt controls, and model sizes against the latency and quality targets.
Draw the critical paths: separate the synchronous generation request from asynchronous ingestion and analytics.
Design the data and evidence: licensing, permitted sources, evaluation prompts, and feedback capture.
Define evaluation and safety: policy checks before and after generation, adversarial suites, and human review.
Operate and improve: plan deployment, monitoring, cost control, incident response, and rollback.

variants.hint: Safety evidence is defined before the serving path is drawn, not after.
variants.explanation: With the contract fixed the chain continues unchanged: data, model, evaluation, architecture, then operations.

variants.title: Work the framework in order
variants.context: The seven-step framework runs from the product contract, through ML framing, data and evidence, model strategy, evaluation and safety, the critical paths, and finally operations. Each step produces an artifact that constrains the next, which is what stops the answer from starting at a model choice.
variants.prompt: You have limited time and the interviewer wants the answer to reach deployment. Put these six steps in order.

items.text: Draw the critical paths and separate synchronous response work from asynchronous loops.
Design the data and evidence, including the evaluation sets that will judge every later choice.
Operate and improve with deployment, monitoring, cost control, and rollback.
Define evaluation and safety so a release decision has evidence behind it.
Select the model strategy by comparing options against the measured constraints.
Frame the ML behavior and name the failure modes worth measuring.

variants.hint: Skipping ahead to architecture leaves the earlier steps with nothing to constrain it.
variants.explanation: Even when compressed, the chain keeps its direction: evaluation sets are designed before the model is chosen, not after it disappoints.

variants.title: Earn the blast radius
variants.context: Passing offline gates earns a bounded exposure, not a launch. Evidence raises the blast radius in stages: offline checks, shadow mode, a small canary with predeclared rollback thresholds, then a gradual rollout watched by real-time monitoring that feeds iteration.
variants.prompt: A candidate model is ready for release. Put the exposure steps in order.

items.text: Feed collected user interactions and feedback into the next iteration of the model.
Run shadow mode against live traffic without showing the candidate output to any user.
Widen to a gradual rollout while real-time safety monitoring watches each increment.
Expose a 1 percent canary with rollback thresholds declared before it starts.
Run the offline gates: task quality, critical safety failures, and cost per successful outcome, kept visible separately.

variants.hint: What has to be true before any user sees the candidate?
variants.explanation: Offline evidence earns a bounded canary, not a global launch, and each stage buys the right to the next one.

variants.title: Earn the blast radius
variants.context: Passing offline gates earns a bounded exposure, not a launch. Evidence raises the blast radius in stages: offline checks, shadow mode, a small canary with predeclared rollback thresholds, then a gradual rollout watched by real-time monitoring that feeds iteration.
variants.prompt: During rollout the candidate starts violating a safety threshold. Put the events in order, ending with what unblocks a retry.

items.text: The canary exposed one percent of traffic behind predeclared rollback thresholds.
The failing cases were added to the evaluation suite before any second attempt.
Real-time safety monitoring recorded violations above the declared threshold.
Shadow mode ran clean, so the candidate was allowed into a bounded canary.
Traffic was rolled back to the incumbent without waiting for a debate about the numbers.

variants.hint: Predeclared thresholds exist so the rollback decision is already made when it is needed.
variants.explanation: A rollback is only useful if the failure becomes evidence, so the incident enters the suite that gates the next candidate.

variants.title: Earn the blast radius
variants.context: Passing offline gates earns a bounded exposure, not a launch. Evidence raises the blast radius in stages: offline checks, shadow mode, a small canary with predeclared rollback thresholds, then a gradual rollout watched by real-time monitoring that feeds iteration.
variants.prompt: A personalized news summarizer must not let stale summaries survive breaking updates. Put its rollout steps in order.

items.text: Shadow the candidate against live breaking-news traffic while users still see the incumbent.
Pass offline factuality and citation checks on a time-based evaluation split.
Expose one percent of a single region and watch stale-summary and correction rates.
Route reader corrections and engagement back into the preference and verification loops.
Widen the rollout in increments while the correction rate stays inside its budget.

variants.hint: Freshness failures show up against live traffic before they show up in a static test set.
variants.explanation: The ladder is the same, but each stage watches the metric this product can actually be harmed by.

variants.title: Spend the budget
variants.context: The product contract carries numbers: first-token and end-to-end latency budgets, traffic estimates, canary percentages, and cost per successful outcome. Each budget is spent by the stages inside it, and cost is judged against outcomes the user accepted, not against raw requests.
variants.prompt: An assistant has a 200 ms end-to-end budget for its first token. Retrieval takes 45 ms, the safety filter takes 25 ms, and network legs take 30 ms. How many milliseconds are left for the model?
variants.hint: Everything inside the budget competes for the same 200 ms.
variants.explanation: The model gets what the other stages leave, so 200 minus 45, 25, and 30 is 100 ms.

mistakes.feedback: That subtracts retrieval only and ignores the safety filter and the network legs.
That adds the stage costs to the budget instead of spending them out of it.

variants.title: Spend the budget
variants.context: The product contract carries numbers: first-token and end-to-end latency budgets, traffic estimates, canary percentages, and cost per successful outcome. Each budget is spent by the stages inside it, and cost is judged against outcomes the user accepted, not against raw requests.
variants.prompt: A service handles 40,000,000 requests a day. The canary runs at 1 percent of one region, and that region carries 25 percent of global traffic. How many requests reach the candidate per day?
variants.hint: The canary percentage applies to the traffic it is actually placed in front of.
variants.explanation: One region carries 10,000,000 requests, and 1 percent of that is 100,000 requests per day.

mistakes.feedback: That applies 1 percent to global traffic and ignores that the canary is scoped to one region.
That is the region's total traffic, which is what the canary would see at 100 percent.

variants.title: Spend the budget
variants.context: The product contract carries numbers: first-token and end-to-end latency budgets, traffic estimates, canary percentages, and cost per successful outcome. Each budget is spent by the stages inside it, and cost is judged against outcomes the user accepted, not against raw requests.
variants.prompt: The suggestion path costs 2 dollars per 1,000 requests, and 20 percent of suggestions are accepted by users. What is the cost per accepted suggestion, in cents?
variants.hint: Cost per successful outcome divides by the outcomes, not by the requests.
variants.explanation: Each request costs 0.2 cents, and only one in five turns into an accepted suggestion, so an acceptance costs 1 cent.

mistakes.feedback: That is the cost per request, which hides how much of the spend produced nothing.
That multiplies by the acceptance rate instead of dividing by it.

variants.title: Let the constraint pick the design
variants.context: An architecture decision is a defensible mapping from the product contract to system boundaries. When latency, privacy, freshness, or scale change, the design changes with them instead of reusing one fashionable stack for every prompt.
variants.prompt: Inline code completion must return in under 50 ms inside the IDE, and repository code must stay inside the promised privacy boundary. Which design follows?
options: Serve a large hosted general model and hide the delay behind a typing animation.
Serve a small specialized model inside the boundary, with a larger tier only for slower paths.
Serve every request through retrieval over the whole repository before generating a token.
optionFeedback: A hidden delay is still a missed budget, and a hosted general model also moves code across the boundary.
Correct: the latency and privacy constraints together select a small in-boundary model with tiering for what can wait.
Whole-repository retrieval on every keystroke spends the 50 ms budget before generation starts.
variants.hint: Two constraints are binding here; a design that satisfies only one is not an answer.
variants.explanation: Latency and privacy constraints jointly select the model tier and its placement, which is what makes the choice defensible.

variants.title: Let the constraint pick the design
variants.context: An architecture decision is a defensible mapping from the product contract to system boundaries. When latency, privacy, freshness, or scale change, the design changes with them instead of reusing one fashionable stack for every prompt.
variants.prompt: Traffic is projected to grow 100x and the generation tier is already GPU bound at peak. What should the design change first?
options: Batch and cache aggressively and route easy requests to a smaller tier.
Buy proportionally more accelerators and keep the serving path unchanged.
Increase the context window so each request can do more work in one call.
optionFeedback: Correct: batching, caching, and tiered routing address the computational bottleneck instead of paying around it.
Linear hardware spend ignores the utilization problem and leaves cost per successful outcome unchanged.
A larger context raises the cost of every request and makes the bottleneck worse.
variants.hint: Which option changes how much work each accelerator does per request?
variants.explanation: Scale answers start at utilization: batching, caching, and tiering before capacity, because they change cost per successful outcome.

variants.title: Let the constraint pick the design
variants.context: An architecture decision is a defensible mapping from the product contract to system boundaries. When latency, privacy, freshness, or scale change, the design changes with them instead of reusing one fashionable stack for every prompt.
variants.prompt: A composer must personalize to each user, but message content may not leave the user's region or enter a shared training corpus. Which approach fits?
options: Personalize with a documented data boundary and techniques whose guarantees match the threat model.
Skip personalization entirely, since any use of message content creates compliance exposure.
Train one global model on message content and delete the raw text after each run.
optionFeedback: Correct: privacy is traced through prompts, retrieval, training, logs, and retention rather than assumed.
Dropping the requirement abandons the product contract instead of designing within it.
Deleting the source afterwards does not remove what the shared model already absorbed.
variants.hint: Where does the content actually travel, and which of those hops does the option control?
variants.explanation: Sensitive data is traced through collection, prompts, retrieval, training, logs, retention, and deletion, and the technique is chosen to match that threat model.

variants.title: Give the question to its step
variants.context: Each of the seven steps owns a distinct set of questions. Requirements own scope and constraints, the ML framing owns inputs, outputs, and success criteria, data owns permissions and evaluation sets, model owns the strategy comparison, quality owns evaluation and safety, system owns the critical paths, and lifecycle owns operations.
variants.prompt: Match each framework step to the artifact it produces.

pairs.label: Requirements
pairs.detail: Users, tasks, modalities, latency, risk, privacy, volume, and explicit non-goals.

pairs.label: Objective
pairs.detail: Inputs, outputs, acceptable uncertainty, retrieval or generation needs, and success criteria.

pairs.label: Data
pairs.detail: Sources, permissions, labeling, freshness, lineage, evaluation sets, and feedback capture.

pairs.label: Model
pairs.detail: A comparison of prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, tool use, and model tiers against measured constraints.

variants.hint: Two of these look similar; one names the product boundary and one names the ML task.
variants.explanation: Each step produces one artifact, and the next step is only answerable because the previous artifact exists.

variants.title: Give the question to its step
variants.context: Each of the seven steps owns a distinct set of questions. Requirements own scope and constraints, the ML framing owns inputs, outputs, and success criteria, data owns permissions and evaluation sets, model owns the strategy comparison, quality owns evaluation and safety, system owns the critical paths, and lifecycle owns operations.
variants.prompt: Match each of the later framework steps to what it owns.

pairs.label: Model
pairs.detail: Benchmarking a small specialized model, a larger fallback, and retrieval-assisted variants against the same gates.

pairs.label: Quality
pairs.detail: Deterministic checks, task metrics, calibrated judges, red teams, and human review.

pairs.label: System
pairs.detail: The split between synchronous response work and asynchronous ingestion, training, and feedback loops.

pairs.label: Lifecycle
pairs.detail: Deployment, monitoring, cost control, incident response, rollback, and evidence-driven iteration.

variants.hint: Only one of these is about drawing boundaries in the request path.
variants.explanation: Evaluation is defined before the architecture is drawn, so the serving design can be justified by measured requirements.

variants.title: Give the question to its step
variants.context: Each of the seven steps owns a distinct set of questions. Requirements own scope and constraints, the ML framing owns inputs, outputs, and success criteria, data owns permissions and evaluation sets, model owns the strategy comparison, quality owns evaluation and safety, system owns the critical paths, and lifecycle owns operations.
variants.prompt: A candidate makes these four statements in an interview. Match each one to the step it belongs to.

pairs.label: Requirements
pairs.detail: We should agree on the first-token budget and who the users are before choosing anything.

pairs.label: Data
pairs.detail: Deletion has to propagate to the index and the evaluation splits, not only the source table.

pairs.label: Quality
pairs.detail: Blinded human review runs beside the automated checks on the adversarial suite.

pairs.label: Lifecycle
pairs.detail: The rollback threshold is declared before the canary starts, not argued about during it.

variants.hint: Ask which artifact each statement would appear in.
variants.explanation: Naming the step a statement belongs to is what keeps an interview answer structured instead of circling one favorite topic.
